faqs.question: How much coffee for a 12-cup coffee maker?

faqs.answer: The Specialty Coffee Association's Golden Cup standard is 55 g of coffee per litre of water, about 1:18. Most home brewers start at 1:17, a touch stronger, because home machines run cooler than certified brewers.
faqs.question: What is the golden ratio for drip coffee?

faqs.answer: The National Coffee Association suggests 1 to 2 tablespoons per 6 oz of water. At 1:17 that works out to about 2 level tablespoons per 6 oz. A scale is more reliable, because a tablespoon of coffee weighs about 5 grams but varies with the roast and the grind.
faqs.question: How many tablespoons of coffee per cup?

faqs.answer: Usually too little coffee or too coarse a grind. Try 1:16 instead of 1:17, and check the grind is medium, like table sugar. Old or stale beans also taste thin, however much you use.

faqs.answer: Yes, a little stronger. Full batches extract less evenly, so 1:15 to 1:16 suits an 8 to 12 cup pot better than 1:17. Start at 1:17 for a half pot and tighten it for a full one.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the coffee
howToSteps.text: Use 14 g per mug at 1:17, or 106 g for a full 12-cup carafe. Grind it medium, like table sugar.

howToSteps.name: Fill the water by weight
howToSteps.text: Weigh the water into the reservoir instead of trusting the cup marks. One litre of water takes 59 g of coffee at 1:17.

howToSteps.name: Brew and wait
howToSteps.text: Start the machine and let it run its full cycle, four to eight minutes. Do not pull the carafe out halfway through to sneak a cup, or the bed floods.

howToSteps.name: Serve straight away
howToSteps.text: Pour the coffee as soon as the cycle ends. Coffee sitting on a hot plate goes stale and bitter within the hour.

title: Drip Machine Coffee to Water Ratio
tutorial: Drip machines do the timing and temperature for you, so the ratio is the one thing you control. Start at 1:17, one gram of coffee for every 17 grams of water. That is 14 g for a single mug and 106 g for a full 12-cup carafe.

The Specialty Coffee Association's Golden Cup standard is 55 g of coffee per litre, about 1:18. Most home machines brew a touch cooler than the certified ideal, so 1:17 is the practical starting point, and many brewers go to 1:16 for a stronger pot. The working range is 1:16 to 1:18.

The cup marks on the carafe are the trap. They are 5 oz each, not 8 oz mugs, so a 12-cup pot holds about 1.8 litres and makes six or seven real mugs. Weigh the water once and write the number on a bit of tape on the machine, and you never have to guess again.

Grind medium, like table sugar. Too fine and the brew stalls and tastes bitter. Too coarse and the water runs through before it has pulled the flavour out, and the coffee tastes thin and sour. A flat-bottom basket and a cone take slightly different grinds, so check your machine's guide.

For a full pot, dose slightly stronger than the ratio says. Big batches extract less evenly, so many brewers use 1:15 or 1:16 for 8 to 12 cups. Start at 1:17 for a half pot and tighten it for a full one, and taste the difference before you settle.
